title_en: Jean Chatzky: How to Create a Forever Paycheck for Retirement
title_zh: Jean Chatzky：如何为退休打造一份永远拿不完的终身支票
subtitle_zh: Jean Chatzky 携新书 The Forever Paycheck 谈如何用年金与收入策略，让退休敢花钱、不缺钱。
summary_zh: 本期 The Long View 由 Morningstar 的 Christine Benz 与 Amy Arnott 主持，对话 hermoney.com CEO、播客 Her Money 主持人 Jean Chatzky，围绕她的新书《The Forever Paycheck》探讨退休支取（decumulation）难题。Chatzky 指出，即便资产充裕，许多退休者仍不敢花钱：一是数学太复杂——应税、延税、Roth 账户交织，还要规避 IRMAA 推高 Medicare 保费或被推入更高税档；二是从积累切到支取存在情绪关卡与'怕花光'的恐惧，且积累端有自动加入、目标日期基金等行为金融助手，支取端却全无。她引入'心理账户'（mental accounting）概念，解释人为何习惯花规律的工资收入、却难以眼看锚定的资产数字下滑，并以母亲继承养老金后的经历为例。方法论上，她对比用总回报组合（total return portfolio）、水桶组合（bucket portfolio）与年金（含可变年金及可能亏损的 RILA，注册指数挂钩型年金）为'终身支票'筹资，主张先认清性情再选工具；也谈到把社会保障金推迟到 70 岁申领、如何搭桥填补空缺，以及回报序列风险（sequence of returns risk）、退休孤独与情感诈骗等问题。是一堂如何让退休敢花钱、不缺钱的实用课。

turns.en: Hi and welcome to the Long View. I'm Christine Benz, Director of Personal Finance and Retirement Planning for Morningstar. And I'm Amy Arnott, Portfolio Strategist for Morningstar.
turns.zh: 嗨，欢迎收听 The Long View。我是 Christine Benz，Morningstar 的个人理财与退休规划总监。我是 Amy Arnott，Morningstar 的组合策略师。

turns.en: Today on the podcast, we welcome back Jean Chatsky. Jean is the author of a new book about retirement planning called The Forever Paycheck, The New Retirement Strategy to Spend More, Worry Less, and Never Run Out of Money.
turns.zh: 本期节目，我们请回了 Jean Chatzky。Jean 刚出了一本关于退休规划的新书，名叫 The Forever Paycheck，副标题是 The New Retirement Strategy to Spend More, Worry Less, and Never Run Out of Money。

turns.en: In addition, she has written several other New York Times bestselling books about money and investing. She's also CEO of hermoney.com and host of the podcast, Her Money with Jean Chatsky.
turns.zh: 此外，她还写过好几本关于金钱和投资的其他 New York Times 畅销书。她还是 hermoney.com 的 CEO，也是播客 Her Money with Jean Chatzky 的主持人。

turns.en: She served as the financial editor of NBC Today for 25 years and is the financial ambassador for AARP. She appears frequently on CNN, MSNBC, and was a recurring guest on the Oprah Winfrey Show.
turns.zh: 她曾在 NBC 的 Today 节目担任财经编辑 25 年，也是 AARP 的财经大使。她经常出现在 CNN、MSNBC 上，还是 Oprah Winfrey Show 的常驻嘉宾。

turns.en: Jean, welcome back to the Long View. Thanks. Thank you so much for having me. Well, thanks for being here and congratulations on your new book, The Forever Paycheck.
turns.zh: Jean，欢迎回到 The Long View。谢谢，非常感谢邀请我来。也谢谢你来到这里，恭喜你出了新书 The Forever Paycheck。

turns.en: We want to delve into the book today. But before we get started with some substantive questions about retirement planning, just wanted to ask what made you want to go deep on this topic of retirement planning?
turns.zh: 我们今天想深入聊聊这本书。不过在抛出那些关于退休规划的实质性问题之前，我们想先问问，是什么让你想深入探究退休规划这个话题的？

turns.en: I think it was a couple of things. I'm 61 years old. And so in the guise of doing a little me search, this is where I've been living lately and where the people that I've grown up with have been living.
turns.zh: 我想有几个原因。我今年 61 岁了。所以做这本有点像寻找自我的书，这也是我最近生活的阶段，也是和我一起长大的那些人所在的阶段。

turns.en: But I also have watched people, including my mother, live in retirement over the past couple of decades and noticed the real difficulty that she and others have had spending their money, which to me seems incredibly sad.
turns.zh: 但过去几十年里，我也看着包括我母亲在内的人如何过日子，注意到她和别人在花钱这件事上有多难，这在我看来真的特别让人难过。

turns.en: We hear, of course, a lot about people who haven't saved enough. But for those who really have done the work and who have set themselves up so beautifully to then find that they just can't open the spigot and live the lives that they had wanted to or planned on living is a real problem.
turns.zh: 我们当然常听说有人存的钱不够。可对于那些确实做了功课、把自己安排得妥妥帖帖的人，到头来却发现根本没法打开水龙头、去过他们一直想过的、计划过的生活，这才是真正的问题。

turns.en: And as somebody who spent so many years writing about accumulating money, investing money, using wealth, it just seemed time to turn to this idea of, OK, what's next?
turns.zh: 作为一个花了这么多年写怎么攒钱、怎么投资、怎么用财富的人，我想是时候转向这个问题了：好，接下来呢？

turns.en: So to expand on that a little bit, why do you think that is that so many people, even retirees who have more than sufficient assets to support their spending, are still reluctant to spend?
turns.zh: 那再展开聊一点，你觉得为什么那么多人——甚至是资产绰绰有余、完全够花的退休者——还是不情愿花钱呢？

turns.en: What do you think are some of the main factors that are contributing to that? I think it's twofold. First, it's really complicated. When you look at the maze of accounts in which we hold our money, taxable, tax deferred, Roth accounts, and the penalties that we could hit if we do it wrong in terms of things like Irma for Medicare or getting kicked into a higher tax bracket, it becomes this very, very difficult math puzzle to figure out how much and what to pull from which accounts
turns.zh: 你觉得主要有哪些因素？我认为是两方面的。第一，它真的很复杂。当你看看我们存钱的那一堆乱七八糟的账户——应税账户、延税账户、Roth 账户——还有万一操作不当会招来的惩罚，比如 IRMAA 让你 Medicare 保费变高，或者被推到更高的税档——这就变成一道极其、极其难的数学题：到底该取多少、从哪个账户取、

turns.en: at what time. There's also a huge amount of fear that if you do it wrong, you'll run out of money. You'll blow through your resources too fast.
turns.zh: 什么时候取。此外还有巨大的恐惧：怕万一取错了，钱就花光了，把家底花得太快。

turns.en: But the other factor is this emotional gait that seems to go up for people when they're asked to flip the switch from accumulation to decumulation.
turns.zh: 另一个因素是，当人们被要求把开关从积累（accumulation）切到支取（decumulation）时，似乎会冒出一道情绪上的坎。

turns.en: It just turns out to be highly uncomfortable. Part of that, I think, is, again, the fear factor. But part of it is that we've gotten so used to saving money for 30, if not 40 years.
turns.zh: 结果就是特别不自在。我觉得一部分原因还是那个恐惧因素，但另一部分是我们太习惯存钱了——存了 30 年，甚至是 40 年。

turns.en: We've bought into this language of paying ourselves first and maxing out our retirement contributions and grabbing all the matching dollars that to ask ourselves to one day just wake up and do the opposite is really, really difficult.
turns.zh: 我们早就接受了那套说法：先付钱给自己、把退休账户的供款拉满、把匹配的钱一分不落都拿满。要让我们某一天醒来突然反着来，真的、真的很难。

turns.en: And while we have these behavioral finance helpers that have been built into the accumulation process, things like auto enrollment and auto escalation of contributions and target date funds to make sure that we're investing appropriately, none of that stuff exists for spending.
turns.zh: 而且在积累这一端，我们已经把一些行为金融学上的帮手内置进去了，比如自动加入、自动上调供款，还有目标日期基金（target date funds）来确保我们投资得当——可这些在花钱这一端统统没有。

turns.en: You had a great section in the book, Jean, where you talk about just the mental accounting aspect of spending income that we're all used to spending income from our paychecks.
turns.zh: Jean，你书里有一段讲得特别好，讲的就是心理账户（mental accounting）的问题——我们都习惯了花工资单上的收入。

turns.en: We're not used to spending from our assets. And I thought that was such a stute point. I'm wondering if you can kind of unpack that for us, because Amy and I have talked between ourselves about how just logistically extracting cash flow from a portfolio with a total return approach, it's harder than just spending dividends.
turns.zh: 我们并不习惯花自己的资产。我觉得这一点特别聪明。你能不能给我们展开讲讲？因为我和 Amy 私底下也聊过，光是从运作层面用总回报（total return）思路从一个组合里提取现金流，就比只花股息要难得多。

turns.en: So maybe these people who are really focused on dividends aren't so irrational. It's just easier to use dividends for your spending money. Can you talk about that issue of income versus assets?
turns.zh: 所以那些一门心思盯着股息的人，也许没那么不理性——拿股息来当零花就是更容易些。你能聊聊收入对比资产这个问题吗？

turns.en: Sure. And there's some really interesting research to back me up. When you're receiving a paycheck, the nice thing about it is the frequency that you know that you got one today, you're going to get another in two weeks, you're going to get another in two weeks again.
turns.zh: 当然。也确实有很有意思的研究支持我的看法。当你领工资时，好处在于那种规律感：你知道今天拿到一笔，两周后还会再拿一笔，再过两周又有一笔。

turns.en: That money is going to keep replenishing itself. And even if you do spend every dime that comes in through that paycheck, there's another where that came from.
turns.zh: 这笔钱会源源不断地补进来。就算你把工资到手的每一分钱都花光了，还会有下一笔跟进。

turns.en: That's not true of assets. When you've got a chunk of money sitting in a retirement account, chances are pretty good that somewhere along the way as you accumulated it, you anchored to a particular number.
turns.zh: 可资产不是这样。当你有一大笔钱躺在退休账户里，很可能在攒钱过程的某个阶段，你就锚定了某个特定的数字。

turns.en: You focused on, I really want to have $1 million for retirement or $2 million for retirement. And maybe you were even successful and you got there.
turns.zh: 你一门心思想着：退休我一定要有 100 万美元，或者 200 万美元。说不定你还真做到了、达到了那个数。

turns.en: Seeing that number then begin to fall is once again really uncomfortable. And I saw this with my mother. So when my mother inherited from my father, my father passed away about 20 years ago.
turns.zh: 眼看着那个数字开始往下掉，又是一件特别让人难受的事。我在我母亲身上就见过。我母亲从我父亲那里继承了财产——我父亲大约 20 年前去世了。

turns.en: My mother was fortunate enough to have his pension because he spent some years as a teacher. She had social security. She had a paid-off apartment.
turns.zh: 我母亲很幸运，有父亲的养老金（pension），因为他当过几年老师。她还有社会保障金（social security），还有一套已经还清贷款的公寓。

turns.en: She had a decent long-term care policy, which was a nice back pocket sort of safety net for her. And then she had this retirement portfolio that was worth $1.6 million.
turns.zh: 她还有一份不错的长期护理保单（long-term care policy），对她来说算是兜里的一张安全网。然后就是那笔价值 160 万美元的退休组合。

turns.en: And she was very, very happy to spend the pension, to spend social security, to spend the income from that $1.6 million. But she didn't want to see that number go down.
turns.zh: 她花养老金、花社会保障金、花那 160 万美元产生的收入，都很开心。可她不想看到那个数字往下掉。

turns.en: And in fact, when she died more than 20 years later, she had a little bit more than that. That's what we're seeing across the board. We're seeing studies point to the fact that many retirees are not spending anything in terms of their principal.
turns.zh: 事实上，20 多年后她去世时，她的钱比那还多了一点。这就是我们普遍看到的现象。研究显示，很多退休者本金一分都没动。

turns.en: Some of them are spending a little bit, but not nearly what they could be. And two noted retirement researchers, folks that I know that you know, Christine and Amy, David Blanchett and Michael Finca, actually did a study where they compared people who had similar-sized wealth.
turns.zh: 有些人花了一点，但远没有到他们本可以花的程度。两位有名的退休研究学者——Christine 和 Amy，你们也认识、我也认识的——David Blanchett 和 Michael Finke，做过一项研究，比较了财富规模相当的人群。

turns.en: But half of the people had the wealth in a pension that was annuitized. It was coming to them every single month in the form of a forever paycheck.
turns.zh: 但其中一半人的财富，是以年金化（annuitized）的养老金形式存在的，每个月以永远发不完的支票的形式打到他们账上。

turns.en: Half of them had the money in a brokerage account. And the people with the paychecks were spending typically twice as much. And the researchers believe that that's simply because they know that there's another paycheck where that one came from, and another after that, and another after that.
turns.zh: 另一半人则把钱放在经纪账户里。而有那种永远支票的人，花销通常是另外一组的两倍。研究者认为，这纯粹是因为他们知道，花掉一笔，下一笔还会来，然后还有再下一笔，一笔接一笔。

turns.en: So for people who do want that type of paycheck equivalent and decide to use an annuity to create that steady income stream, what process should people be going through to research and purchase an annuity as well as making sure that the insurer is financially strong?
turns.zh: 那么，对于确实想要这种等同于永远支票、并决定用年金（annuity）来打造这种稳定收入流的人，他们在研究和购买年金、以及确认保险公司财务稳健时，应该走一个什么样的流程呢？

turns.en: So before we get to that, I would never suggest that people take all of their money and put it into an annuity. This is a solution for the money that you need in combination with social security to cover your needs and your important wants, the things that you really don't want to live without.
turns.zh: 在说那个之前，我绝不会建议有人把全部的钱都投进年金。这是一个解决方案，用来配合社会保障金，覆盖你的必需开支和那些重要的想要——就是你生活里真的不能没有的那些东西。

turns.en: Typically, it's about 20% to 30% of your money. You can think of it as the component of your portfolio that you have in fixed income rather than in equities or in stocks.
turns.zh: 通常大约是你资金的 20% 到 30%。你可以把它想成你组合里配置在固定收益（fixed income）而不是股票上的那部分。

turns.en: But everybody needs the growth of the market in retirement. You still need to keep a hand in the market, assets in the market, a significant amount because you need that growth to keep up with taxes and inflation.
turns.zh: 但每个人在退休时都需要市场的增长。你仍然要在市场里留一手，要有一笔可观的资产留在市场里，因为你需要那种增长来跟上税收和通胀。

turns.en: Once you've decided that you want to paycheck, if you want to create it using an annuity, there are a number of steps you need to go through.
turns.zh: 一旦你下定决心想要那份永远支票，如果想用年金来打造它，就得走好几步。

turns.en: You have to figure out what type of annuity. There are a number of different products out there, but they boil down to fixed and variable. The fixed annuities have a guarantee that you are never going to lose principal.
turns.zh: 你得先弄清要买哪种年金。市面上的产品五花八门，但归根结底就是固定型（fixed）和可变型（variable）两大类。固定年金有一个保证：你永远不会亏本金。

turns.en: You may not make a ton in some years, depending on how this annuity is baked, but you know that there's this guarantee that you're never going to lose money.
turns.zh: 有些年份你可能赚不了多少，取决于这份年金怎么烘焙出来的，但你心里清楚有一条保证：绝不会亏钱。

turns.en: Variable annuities and what are called RILAS, registered index-linked annuities, have an investment component that is tied to a market index and in those, you can lose money.
turns.zh: 可变年金，还有所谓 RILA（registered index-linked annuities，注册指数挂钩型年金），里面有一个和市场指数挂钩的投资成分，这类产品你是可能亏钱的。

turns.en: How much depends on how that annuity is once again put together, but you have to decide what kind of product you want. And then you go through a process of shopping.
turns.zh: 会亏多少，同样取决于那份年金怎么搭建，但你得先决定自己想要哪种产品，然后就要去货比三家。

turns.en: And this is not something that you're likely to do yourself. You certainly can go on the Internet. There are a number of different sites like immediateannuities.com and annuities.com and Stan the annuity man that have calculators and the ability to price out some simple annuities much like you'd price out life insurance on the web.
turns.zh: 而这不太是你自己一个人能搞定的。你当然可以上网。有好几个不同的网站，比如 immediateannuities.com、annuities.com，还有 Stan the Annuity Man，它们都有计算器，能给一些简单的年金报价，就像你在网上给人身寿险报价一样。

turns.en: And that's not at all a bad place to start, but eventually you're going to want to talk to a financial advisor or an insurance agent who can walk you through the different products that are available on the market today.
turns.zh: 作为起点这完全不算坏，但到最后，你会想跟一位财务顾问或保险经纪人好好谈谈，让他带你梳理一遍当今市面上能买到的各种产品。

turns.en: You're going to compare them by their various features. What are you getting in terms of a return? What are the guarantees? Is there a cost of living increase built in?
turns.zh: 你要按各种特性把它们比较一番。回报率能有多少？有哪些保证？有没有内置生活成本调整（cost of living increase）？

turns.en: Is there what's called a return of premium guarantee, which means that the amount of money that you put in, you or your heirs will get back?
turns.zh: 有没有所谓的已缴保费返还保证（return of premium guarantee），也就是说你投进去的那笔钱，你或你的继承人能拿回来？

turns.en: All of those things factor into the pricing of whatever product you're looking at, but you want to make sure that you're comparing apples to apples from different companies.
turns.zh: 所有这些都会影响你在看的产品的定价，但你要确保拿不同公司的产品做同口径的比较。

turns.en: And then it's really important to look at the quality of the underwriter, the rating of the insurance company itself as with life insurance, as with bonds.
turns.zh: 然后，承保人的品质——也就是保险公司本身的评级——非常关键，就像挑人身寿险、挑债券一样。

turns.en: There are ratings agencies, many of the same ratings agencies that will give the insurer a letter grade. And you want to stick with those insurers that are in the A category.
turns.zh: 有评级机构，其中很多就是给发行人打级的那几家，它们会给保险公司一个字母等级。你要认准那些处在 A 类的保险公司。

turns.en: I would not go into the B category for something as important as this. So Jean, we have lots more questions about annuities, but first I wanted to discuss the fact that there seem to be two factions in the space of guaranteed income, where a lot of my Boglehead's friends would say, forget the annuity.
turns.zh: 对这么要紧的东西，我是不会去碰 B 类的。那么 Jean，关于年金我们还有很多问题，但首先我想聊一个现象：在保证收入这块，似乎有两派，我的很多 Bogleheads 朋友会说，别买年金了。

turns.en: You should just do a laddered portfolio of treasury inflation protected securities tip spawns, where you do have that built-in CPI adjustment.
turns.zh: 你只要搭一个国债通胀保值证券（TIPS）的阶梯组合（laddered portfolio）就行了，那里头本来就有 CPI 调整。

turns.en: You don't have longevity protection, but can you compare and contrast those two different approaches to securing quasi-guaranteed income and retirement?
turns.zh: 只是没有长寿保障（longevity protection），不过你能把这两种获取准保证收入的退休思路做个对比吗？

turns.en: Absolutely, and I think there are a lot of people like your Boglehead's friends who are going to want to build their forever paycheck, if they want one, with investments rather than with insurance.
turns.zh: 当然。我想有很多像你那些 Bogleheads 朋友一样的人，如果他们想要一份永远支票，会更愿意用投资、而不是用保险来打造它。

turns.en: It basically comes down to two considerations. Number one is how much of a guarantee is important to you. You can do an awful lot with ladders.
turns.zh: 归根到底是两个考量。第一，有多大保证对你有多重要。阶梯策略能做很多事。

turns.en: But one thing that you can't do is predict the future of interest rates. And when rungs roll off that ladder, the money needs to be reinvested.
turns.zh: 但有件事你做不到：预测未来的利率。当阶梯里的一根根横档到期滚动出来时，那笔钱得再投出去。

turns.en: And if rates have shifted in a way that is not great for income, that is a risk that you're going to have to live with. On the flip side, there are guarantees available with insurance that you can lock into for life.
turns.zh: 如果利率的变化方向对收入不利，那你就得承受这个风险。反过来看，保险这边有你能锁定一辈子的保证。

turns.en: The returns will vary. You have to compare the returns that you're going to get from those laddered tips or those laddered bonds or CDs against what you're likely to get with insurance, but it's another way to go.
turns.zh: 回报率会有高低。你得把那种 TIPS 阶梯、或者债券、CD（存单）阶梯能给你的回报，跟保险大概率给你的回报做个比较，但它确实是另一条路。

turns.en: The other factor that plays into this is how much of a feeling of FOMO or fear of missing out you have in your personality. If the markets do incredibly well and you've locked up a chunk of your money in an annuity that's only going to pay you a certain amount, are you going to be kicking yourself every single day?
turns.zh: 另一个起作用的因素，是你性格里有多少 FOMO、也就是错失恐惧（fear of missing out）的成分。如果市场涨得特别好，而你把一大笔钱锁在一份只按固定数额付钱的年金里，你会不会天天拍大腿后悔？

turns.en: If you are, then you're probably better off trying to fund your paycheck with investments. And in the book, I explained how you can do this with a total return portfolio, how you could do this with a bucket portfolio, how you could do it with annuities that do have a leg in the market.
turns.zh: 如果你会，那你多半更适合用投资来给你的支票筹钱。我在书里解释了怎么用总回报组合（total return portfolio）来做、怎么用水桶组合（bucket portfolio）来做、以及怎么用那种在市场里也留了一条腿的年金来做。

turns.en: And so you need to understand who you are and how you're wired in order to figure out how to best create a paycheck for yourself. So one trend we've been hearing a lot about in the annuity space is the fact that there are a lot of private equity-backed insurance companies who have been investing their reserve assets in private credits.
turns.zh: 所以你得认清自己、了解自己天生的性情，才能找出最适合自己的方式去打造那份支票。那么年金这块我们常听到的一个趋势是：有很多由私募股权（private equity）控股的保险公司，把它们的准备金资产投进了私募信贷（private credit）。

turns.en: Is that something that annuity buyers should be worried about and is there a way for people to avoid the potential problems related to that?
turns.zh: 这是年金买家该担心的事吗？有没有办法让人规避与之相关的潜在问题？

turns.en: So you're right that life insurers have been big participants in private credit and they have figured out a way to make use of it in the portfolio.
turns.zh: 你说得没错，人身险公司一直是私募信贷的重要参与者，它们也找到了在组合里加以利用的办法。

turns.en: The question is, how much transparency you have into what sits inside that portfolio? Generally, this is more of a caution with those annuities that are linked to market performance, the ones that actually can lose value, the variable annuities, the registered index-linked annuities, the RILAs.
turns.zh: 问题在于：你对组合里头装的是什么有多透明？一般来说，这种警惕更多是针对那些与市场表现挂钩的年金——也就是真会贬值的——可变年金、注册指数挂钩型年金，也就是 RILA。

turns.en: The fixed annuities, which again, there are many types of these, are not market loss products. And so as long as you lock into an annuity provider, a carrier that is top rated, I think that you're going to be fine.
turns.zh: 固定年金，同样也是有很多种，并不是会因市场亏损的产品。所以只要你锁定一家评级顶尖的年金提供商、承保机构，我想你不会有问题。

turns.en: But as far as those variable products, I think you do want to know what's in the portfolio. And I think that that is something that is a perfectly reasonable question to ask anybody that you're working with to buy an annuity.
turns.zh: 但就那些可变产品而言，我确实觉得你该知道组合里装的是什么。而且我认为，这是一个完全合理的问题，可以问你合作买年金的任何人。

turns.en: In the book, you talk about the value of getting some financial advice, some kind of a planner or something like that. How would you recommend that investors navigate finding the right person if they are compelled by this idea of an annuity?
turns.zh: 你在书里谈到获取一些财务建议、找一位规划师之类的价值。如果投资者被年金这个主意打动了，你会建议他们怎么去找对的人呢？

turns.en: How do they find a partner to help them navigate? In my experience, a lot of planners would be like, oh, I don't really touch insurance products at all.
turns.zh: 他们怎么找到一个能帮他们引路的伙伴？据我了解，很多规划师会说，哦，我根本不碰保险产品。

turns.en: So how do you find someone who's conversant in all of these issues? Well, this happened to me. I have a financial advisor. I've had a financial advisor the same one for many, many years.
turns.zh: 那你怎么找到一个精通所有这些问题的专家？我本人就遇到过这事。我有位财务顾问，这么多年我一直用同一位。

turns.en: I'm generally a very, very happy customer. But as I went through the research for this book, I became more and more convinced that actually, I do want a forever paycheck.
turns.zh: 总体来讲，我这个客户非常满意。但在我为这本书做调研的过程中，我越来越确信：其实我是想要一份永远支票的。

turns.en: And based on my personality, I'm going to fund that forever paycheck or part of that forever paycheck with an annuity. And I went to my financial advisor and I said, let's talk about this.
turns.zh: 以我的性格，我打算用一份年金来为那份永远支票——或者它的一部分——筹钱。于是我去找我的财务顾问，说：咱们来聊聊这事。

turns.en: And he wouldn't help me. He said, we just don't do this. And what I learned in interviewing financial advisors is that they tend to lock into a particular methodology, many of them.
turns.zh: 可他不肯帮我。他说：我们就是不做这个。我在采访各位财务顾问时了解到，他们当中很多人往往会死守某一种方法论。

turns.en: If they're total return people, then that's what they're going to do for you. If they're bucket people, then that's what they're going to do for their clients.
turns.zh: 如果他们是做总回报那一派的，那他们就会给你做那一套；如果是水桶派的，那他们就照着这套给客户做。

turns.en: And so you are going to want to ask outright the question if you are unable to get this from your own advisor, you're going to want to ask other advisors.
turns.zh: 所以你得开门见山地直接问。如果你自己的顾问这边拿不到，你就要去问别的顾问。

turns.en: Is this the type of product that you can help me with? I went through an exercise of asking people that I trust for recommendations of advisors who work in the annuity space and have been going through a process of evaluating a few of them and the different types of products that they are suggesting for me.
turns.zh: 问：这是你能帮我做的产品类型吗？我就做过这么一件事——向我信任的人打听，请他们推荐那些在年金领域做事的顾问，然后一直在评估其中几位、以及他们给我建议的各种产品。

turns.en: But I would not be at all surprised if you find yourself in that situation. And I also think it's fine to divide and conquer. I'm going to stay with my advisor.
turns.zh: 但如果你也落到这种境地，我一点都不会意外。而且我觉得分而治之也完全没问题：我打算继续跟着我的顾问。

turns.en: I'm very happy with the work that he's done for me. But I've also told him I'm taking a chunk of my money and I'm using it to do this. We also wanted to spend some time talking about other sources of income like social security or portfolio withdrawals.
turns.zh: 他为我做的工作，我非常满意。但我也告诉他，我要拿出一笔钱来做这件事。我们也想花点时间聊聊其他收入来源，比如社会保障金或者组合提取（portfolio withdrawals）。

turns.en: And you write in the book that waiting to file for social security until age 70 is the best course of action for many people, especially people who are in good health, who expect to live long enough to get the full advantage of those higher social security payments.
turns.zh: 你在书里写到，对很多人来说，把申领社会保障金推迟到 70 岁是最佳选择，尤其是那些身体好、预期活得够久、能把更高额的社会保障金领个够的人。

turns.en: But if you are waiting to claim social security, you're kind of faced with a gap between when you retire and when you start getting those checks.
turns.zh: 可如果你在等着申领社会保障金，那你退休到开始领那笔支票之间，就面临一个空缺。

turns.en: Can you talk about some strategies for bridging that gap between when you retire and when you actually start receiving social security? Yeah, absolutely.
turns.zh: 你能不能讲讲，怎么搭桥填上从退休到真正开始领社会保障金之间的那段空缺？嗯，当然可以。

turns.en: One strategy is just to continue to work a little bit. We're seeing more and more people phasing into retirement. And although there are some penalties, if you earn too much money, keeping a certain amount of income flowing in can help bridge the gap.
turns.zh: 一个策略就是继续工作一小段时间。我们看到越来越多的人在逐步过渡退休。虽然收入太高会有一些惩罚性扣减，但保持一定金额的收入进来，能帮你填平那段空缺。

turns.en: It may pay to pull money out of some retirement accounts in order to bridge the gap from when you stop working until you file for social security.
turns.zh: 从你停止工作、直到申领社会保障金之间，为了填这段空缺，从某些退休账户里取钱也许反而划算。

turns.en: What you have to keep in mind is that each year you wait to take social security generally equates to about a 7% to 8% bump in what you'll get in your monthly check.
turns.zh: 你要记住的是：晚领社会保障金，每推迟一年，通常意味着你每月那笔支票大约能多 7% 到 8%。

turns.en: If you have other places that you can pull the money from, then it often pays just to wait for that money to grow, especially because social security is a program that has a real cost of living adjustment.
turns.zh: 如果你有别的地方可以取钱，那么往往干脆等这笔钱往上长更划算，尤其是因为社会保障金这个项目有真正的生活成本调整（cost of living adjustment）。

turns.en: It actually adjusts with whatever the inflation rate is each year. And that was hugely helpful over the past couple of years as inflation spiked.
turns.zh: 它每年都会跟着当年的通胀率来调整。过去几年通胀飙升的时候，这一点帮了大忙。

turns.en: So you can look at pulling money out of your other retirement accounts. If your income drops significantly, it actually can be a fairly good time to pull money out of your tax deferred accounts, because you may be able to pay taxes at a lower rate or in a lower bracket.
turns.zh: 所以你可以考虑从其他退休账户里取钱。如果你的收入大幅下降，那其实是从延税账户取钱的挺好时机，因为你也许能按更低的税率、或更低的税档来缴税。

turns.en: And you can also look at using what people call a bridge annuity, which is a simple income annuity that you buy not forever, but for the certain number of years between the time that you stop earning and start taking social security.
turns.zh: 你还可以考虑用所谓过桥年金（bridge annuity），也就是一份简单的收入型年金，你买的不是永远，而是覆盖你从停止赚钱到开始领社会保障金之间那段特定的年数。

turns.en: So you might buy a simple income annuity that lasts for five years, if that's how long you expect that period of time to be. As a financial advisor, you've got your clients back and we've got yours.
turns.zh: 比如，如果你觉得那段空缺是五年，你可能就买一份为期五年的简单收入型年金。身为财务顾问，你为客户保驾护航，而我们也为你保驾护航。

turns.en: With Vanguard's actively managed bond funds, you're backed by consistent performance with a low cost edge for an advantage that keeps compounding and compounding and compounding.
turns.zh: 有了 Vanguard 主动管理的债券基金，你就有稳健的业绩和低费率优势作后盾，这份优势会不断复利、不断复利、不断复利。

turns.en: Sorry, quick break for legal. To learn more, visit vanguard.com. All investing is subject to risk. Investments and bonds are subject to interest rate, credit and inflation risk, Vanguard Marketing Corporation distributor.
turns.zh: 抱歉，插播一段法律免责声明。想了解更多，请访问 vanguard.com。所有投资都有风险。投资与债券面临利率风险、信用风险和通胀风险。Vanguard Marketing Corporation，分销商。

turns.en: Are you backed by institutional quality bond funds? Vanguard. So another issue that people face when they're getting close to retirement is sequence of returns risk.
turns.zh: 有机构级品质的债券基金为你护航吗？Vanguard。那么，人们在临近退休时面临的另一个问题，就是回报序列风险（sequence of returns risk）。

turns.en: And this is probably top of mind for a lot of people, just given that the market has been doing so well for so long. Do you have any advice for people who are thinking about retiring but worried that they might be retiring into a very poor market in the years ahead?
turns.zh: 考虑到市场已经涨得这么好、涨了这么久，这大概是很多人心里最惦记的事。对那些正在考虑退休、却担心自己会退休进未来几年一个很差的行情的人，你有什么建议吗？

turns.en: We haven't really touched on the 4% rule in this conversation yet, but the sequence of returns risk goes sort of part and parcel with the 4% rule and is a big reason why the 4% rule has come under fire and why Morningstar has started to issue a new number each year for what that initial portfolio withdrawal should be.
turns.zh: 我们这场对话里还没怎么聊到 4% 法则（4% rule），但回报序列风险跟 4% 法则其实是形影不离的，也正是 4% 法则备受质疑的一大原因——这也是为什么 Morningstar 开始每年都给出一个新的数字，来说明退休第一年那笔初始提取该是多少。

turns.en: Sequence of returns risk is essentially the problem of hitting a down market in the couple of years right before or the couple of years right after retirement.
turns.zh: 回报序列风险，本质上就是在退休前几年或退休后头几年正好撞上下跌行情的问题。

turns.en: And what happens is that if your balance dips that much or dips significantly and you are pulling too much out of your portfolio in those initial years of withdrawal, you are at a greater risk of running out of money down the road.
turns.zh: 结果就是：如果你的余额大幅下滑，而你在开始提取的头几年又从组合里取走了太多，那你往后把钱花光的风险就更大。

turns.en: And considering that that's the fear that keeps people up at night, it's no wonder that this is something that's on a whole lot of people's minds.
turns.zh: 考虑到这正是让人夜里睡不着觉的那种恐惧，难怪这么多人都把它放在心上。

turns.en: I mean, my advice would be if this is what you want to do, if this is how you are planning to fund your retirement, then as you enter retirement, I'd turn right to Morningstar.
turns.zh: 我的建议是：如果这就是你想做的，如果你就打算靠这套来给退休筹钱，那么在你进入退休的时候，我劝你直接去看 Morningstar。

turns.en: I mean, you guys are issuing a number each year. As I've been following it, it's ranged from about 3.3% up to 4% of what you can safely withdraw in the first year of retirement.
turns.zh: 我是说，你们每年都给出一个数字。就我一直在跟踪的情况看，它大致在 3.3% 到 4% 之间——也就是退休第一年你能安全提取的比例。

turns.en: If you follow that guidance and then you adjust with inflation each year following, you should be OK. One thing Amy and I have concluded in working on that research, Jean, and thank you for the shout out is just that if people can be flexible with their spending from year to year, that is kind of a best practice in terms of portfolio spending.
turns.zh: 如果你照着那个指引来，然后在往后的每一年都跟着通胀调整，你多半没问题。Jean，我和 Amy 在做那项研究时得出的一个结论——也谢谢你的点名——就是：如果人们能在每年的开销上保持灵活，那在组合支取这件事上，基本就算是一种最佳实践了。

turns.en: And I don't know if you agree, but to me, that goes hand in hand with securing as much sort of steady income as you can. Like if you have more steady income, then you can be flexible.
turns.zh: 不知道你是否同意，但在我看来，这跟你尽可能多地锁定稳定收入是相辅相成的。就是说，如果你有越多稳定收入，你就越能灵活。

turns.en: Do you tend to concur with that approach? 100%, I think if you know, there are some things that are very, very difficult to be flexible on. Your Medicare premiums, very hard to be flexible.
turns.zh: 你认同这个做法吗？百分之百认同。我觉得，有些东西是非常、非常难有弹性的。你的 Medicare 保费，就很难弹性调整。

turns.en: Your housing costs if you have been living in the same place and you have a pretty steady property tax bill, you know, general upkeep, food and utilities and all of those things that fall under the category of needs.
turns.zh: 你的住房成本——如果你一直住在同一个地方，房产税账单也相对稳定——还有日常维护、吃饭、水电煤气，所有这些归在必需这一类的东西。

turns.en: It's very, very tough to be flexible when it comes to those things. When it comes to the second vacation, when it comes to the number of times you go out to dinner in a particular week, we are able to flex.
turns.zh: 在这些事情上，想要有弹性真的非常非常难。但要说第二次度假、要说你一周里头下几次馆子，这些我们是能弹性调整的。

turns.en: And what I have seen from the massive spending database that the folks at JP Morgan Chase maintain because they follow the flows of money that people spend on their credit cards, their data shows that retirees are flexible, that in years when the markets are down, specifically around the Great Recession, people did spend less.
turns.zh: 我从 JP Morgan Chase 那边维护的海量消费数据库里也看到了这一点，因为他们追踪人们刷信用卡花掉的钱的流向。他们的数据显示，退休者确实是有弹性的：在市场下跌的年份，尤其是在大衰退（Great Recession）前后，人们确实花得更少。

turns.en: What I think is the benefit of having your fixed expenses and some of your wants covered by income that you know is guaranteed in the form of a forever paycheck is that it gives you the ability not to have to flex on everything.
turns.zh: 我觉得，让那些以永远支票形式保证的收入，去覆盖你的固定开支和一部分想要，它的好处就在于：它让你不必事事都去压缩。

turns.en: It gives you the ability to know, yeah, okay, I'm still going to be able to go on that first vacation a year with my family. Maybe the second one is something that we won't do, but I know I have the first one covered.
turns.zh: 它让你心里有底：嗯，好，我一年到头还是能跟家人去第一次度假。也许第二次就不去了，但我知道第一次是保得住的。

turns.en: I know my gym membership, which I really do not want to have to compromise on, is covered. If you can lock in to knowing that you've got a certain amount of money that will last you as long as you live that will cover those things, I think that's a very nice way to be able to put your mind at ease as you enter retirement.
turns.zh: 我知道我的健身房会员费——这是我真不想将就的一项——是覆盖得住的。如果你能锁定这样一份确定：有一笔钱能伴随你一生、把这些都覆盖住，那我觉得，在你进入退休时，这是让自己安心的一种很好的方式。

turns.en: I wanted to transition into talking about some more lifestyle related issues for retirement and one interesting stat that you quoted in the book kind of jumped out at me and that was only six out of 10 couples share the same vision of retirement or vision for retirement.
turns.zh: 我想转到退休里一些更偏生活方式的话题。你在书里引的一个有意思的数据特别打动我：只有六成的夫妻，对退休有相同的愿景、或者说相同的退休构想。

turns.en: Can you talk about other ways to talk to your spouse and kind of bridge the gap if you do have a different vision or is there a good way for each person to maybe get part of what they want?
turns.zh: 你能不能讲讲，如果两人确实有不同的愿景，有什么别的办法去跟配偶沟通、去弥合这段差距？或者说，有没有一种好办法，让彼此都能各自得到一部分想要的？

turns.en: I think talking about it has to be the goal and what that research and other research has shown is that a lot of people don't talk about it and not only do they not talk about it with their partners, they don't really plot it out themselves. They haven't figured out what retirement is going to look like when it's going to begin, where they're going to live it, what they're going to do on a random Tuesday afternoon and until you actually start thinking about those more mundane touch
turns.zh: 我觉得，把它说出来就必须是目标。而那份研究以及其他研究都表明：很多人根本不去谈。他们不但没跟伴侣谈，自己也没真正盘算过。他们没想清楚退休到底会是什么样子——什么时候开始、在哪里过、在一个随机的周二下午要做什么。而直到你真正开始去想这些更琐碎的具

turns.en: points and then line them up with your spouse, I don't know how anybody comes up with an estimate for what their retirement is going to cost because depending on your vision for it, the price tag could be wildly, wildly different. I have clipped and saved an article from The Wall Street Journal, I wrote about this in the book, a woman, a reporter years ago wrote an article with the headline, He Says Mean, She Says Florida and it was all about how she and her husband had never
turns.zh: 体节点、再把它们跟你的配偶对齐，我真不明白任何人是怎么估算出退休要花多少钱的——因为取决于你对退休的构想，那个价码可能天差地别。我剪存过一篇 The Wall Street Journal 的文章，我在书里也写过这事：多年前一位女记者写了一篇文章，标题叫 He Says Maine, She Says Florida，讲的就是她和她丈夫从来没有

turns.en: had the conversation about what are they going to do and when they finally did have the conversation, she wanted to see the world and he wanted to spend his days going to the public library three blocks from where they lived. I mean, the visions could not have been more different.
turns.zh: 好好谈过他们到底要过什么样的日子。等到他们终于坐下来谈，她想去看看世界，而他想过的日子，是每天去离他们住处三个街区远的那家公共图书馆。我的天，两个人的愿景能差到不能再差。

turns.en: Eventually, they came to a bit of a compromise. I called her as I was reporting this book and said what happened and she said, well, he goes on the trips that he wants to go on. I go on more trips than he does, but we've kind of learned to divide and conquer and I think that for many retirees, particularly as we live longer, is going to be a key to happiness. There are trips that I want to go on that I know my husband doesn't want to go on, but I'm going to go with my girlfriends.
turns.zh: 最后，他们达成了一点妥协。我在为这本书做采访时给她打了电话，问后来怎么样了。她说：他想去的旅行他就去，我则比他去更多趟，我们算是学会了分头行动。我觉得，对很多退休者来说，尤其是随着我们活得更久，这会是一个通往幸福的关键。有些旅行我想去，可我知道我丈夫不想去，那我就和闺蜜们一起去。

turns.en: There are things, experiences that he would like to have a certain number of baseball tickets every single year. I'll go to one game, right? Give me a hot dog and a beer, one game a year and I am happy, but he's going to have to find somebody else to enjoy those games with and that's okay. He can come back and he can tell me about them after.
turns.zh: 也有一些他想拥有的体验，比如每年弄若干张棒球赛的票。我会去看一场，对吧？给我一根热狗、一杯啤酒，一年一场我就心满意足了。可剩下的比赛，他就得另找人一起享受，这没关系。他可以看完回来跟我讲讲。

turns.en: We had David Bach on the podcast earlier this year and he made a provocative point that's kind of stuck with me. We were talking about the go-go, slo-go, no-go phases of retirement and he argues that for some men, it's a won't-go kind of mindset that they retire to the couch.
turns.zh: 今年早些时候我们请过 David Bach 上节目，他提了一个挺有冲击力、一直让我记着的观点。我们当时在聊退休的 go-go、slow-go、no-go 三个阶段，他说，对有些男人而言，那其实是一种 won't-go 的心态——他们一退休就退到沙发上去了。

turns.en: I'm wondering if you can talk about whether you're seeing that in any of the data and also how men, women, I suppose it could cut across genders, how they can make sure that that's not them if they don't want it to be them. I've heard David say this, which is so the opposite of David.
turns.zh: 我想知道你能不能聊聊，你在数据里有没有看到这种情况；还有男人、女人——我想这可能不分性别——如果他们不想成为那种人，该怎么确保自己不是那样。我也听 David 说过这个说法，这跟 David 本人可太相反了。

turns.en: You know David Bach and I know him very well and he wants to ski 100 days a year, so I'm not exactly sure where he's getting this, but I do think part of the issue is a loneliness issue and a friendship issue and I've seen a lot of research on the very few number of friends that men have compared to women. When you retire, you need people to do things with and if you have very few friendships, that makes it hard to find playmates to
turns.zh: 你认识 David Bach，我跟他很熟。他一年想滑 100 天雪，所以我不太确定他这套是从哪儿来的。不过我确实认为，这问题的一部分是孤独问题、是友谊问题。我看过很多研究，说男人跟女人比起来，朋友少得可怜。退休以后，你需要有人一起做事；如果你的朋友圈很窄，那你就很难找到玩伴陪你一起去

turns.en: pal along on these adventures that you may want to have or to encourage you to get up and get off the couch and so I think if you sense that you might be this type of person or that your spouse might be this type of person before retirement is when you want to start encouraging them to be a little bit more of a joiner to pick up some sort of a hobby that involves other people to look into classes at the local university that they might be able to audit
turns.zh: 冒险，或者鼓励你从沙发上爬起来、动起来。所以我觉得，如果你隐约觉得自己可能是这种人，或者你的配偶可能是这种人，那在退休之前，你就该开始鼓励他们多合群一点：培养某种要跟别人打交道的爱好，去打听打听本地大学里那些他们可以旁听的课程，

turns.en: to think about volunteering or mentoring or just something where they are going to very, very frequently see other people besides you because loneliness in retirement is a huge issue.
turns.zh: 去考虑做志愿者、做导师，或者找一件让他们能非常、非常频繁地见到你以外别人的事，因为退休中的孤独是一个大问题。

turns.en: And it's very difficult to fight it if you don't have the right networks going in. You also touched earlier on people who actually go back to work after retiring either full-time or in some sort of part-time or consulting capacity and some of those people might be doing that for financial reasons, but there are also a lot of non-financial reasons that people decide to continue working or start working again. Can you talk a little bit more about what work
turns.zh: 如果你进来时没有合适的人脉网络，想对抗孤独会非常难。你前面也提到有些人退休后还真会重返工作岗位——要么全职，要么以某种兼职或顾问的身份。这些人里有些是出于财务原因，但也有很多非财务的原因，让人决定继续工作或者重新开始工作。你能不能多聊聊，工作

turns.en: can add in terms of the quality of life for people who might be retirement age? I think work can add a social element. It gives you the opportunity to interact with other people.
turns.zh: 能给到了退休年龄的人的生活质量带来些什么？我觉得，工作能增添一种社交成分，它给你机会去和别人互动。

turns.en: It also, this may be generational, but I sit right on the bubble of Baby Boomer and Gen X, and I think that this generation of people about to head into retirement is very, very attached in an ego way to work. Work feeds their ego. It's a constant source for many people of affirmation. Continuing to work, finding some way to stay connected to that life, means that that part of you continues to get fed. And for people who are afraid of retirement,
turns.zh: 还有一点，这可能跟代际有关——我正好处在婴儿潮一代（Baby Boomer）和 X 一代（Gen X）的分界线上。我觉得即将退休的这一代人，在一种自我的层面上非常、非常依恋工作。工作滋养他们的自尊，对很多人来说，它是持续的肯定感来源。继续工作、想办法跟那种生活保持连接，就意味着你那部分自我能一直得到滋养。而对于那些害怕退休的人，

turns.en: and I'm one of them, I think that that is something to think very, very hard about. How are you going to handle the loss of that source of good feelings, and is there a way to keep a foot in the door? I don't think that you can discount the financial reasons, too. I mean, having a little bit of money coming in means that you can pull a little bit less out of your retirement funds. It means that those retirement funds can continue to grow. It may mean that you can help
turns.zh: 我自己就是其中之一，我觉得这一点真的要非常非常好好想清楚。你打算如何应对那份美好感受来源的丧失？有没有办法一只脚还留在门里？我觉得也不能小看财务上的原因。我的意思是，有一点钱进来，就意味着你可以从退休金里少取一点，意味着那笔退休金能继续增长，也意味着你也许能帮

turns.en: your adult children without feeling like it's a stressor. And if you're trying to delay social security, it can help with that, too. And so I think there are reasons on both sides of the ledger to think about continuing to work.
turns.zh: 帮衬已成年的子女，而不会觉得是个负担。如果你在设法推迟申领社会保障金，这也帮得上忙。所以我觉得，账本两边都有理由支持你考虑继续工作。

turns.en: Jean, I wanted to ask you about something that I've been thinking a lot about lately, which is the risks of scams and frauds and cognitive decline that we all might run into as we age, especially. And I'm wondering if you can talk about, as you think about those things, what are kind of best practices for people who want to help safeguard themselves and their money against some of those risks? I've seen these studies as well, and it's very, very frightening,
turns.zh: Jean，我想问你一件我最近一直在琢磨的事，就是我们上了年纪后都可能遭遇的诈骗、欺诈和认知衰退的风险。我想知道，在你思考这些问题的时候，对那些想保护自己和自己的钱、抵御其中一些风险的人，有没有什么最佳实践？这些研究我也看过，真的非常、非常吓人，

turns.en: both that cognitive decline shows up in our financial lives often and also well before we get a diagnosis of being in cognitive decline. It's often as much as five to 10 years before the diagnosis hits. And this is where I think family and financial advisors become really important. There comes a point in your life where you have to say to your kids or to an advisor, I know I'm getting older. This is an issue. It's an issue that I've read about.
turns.zh: 认知衰退往往在我们财务生活中早早显现，而且远早于我们被诊断出认知衰退。往往在确诊之前 5 到 10 年就已经出现了。而我觉得这正是家人和财务顾问变得非常关键的地方。人生总有一个时刻，你得对孩子或者对顾问说：我知道我在变老，这是个问题，是我读到过的问题。

turns.en: It's an issue that other people are experiencing. If you start to see any behaviors in me or in my life that worry you, you should say something. You can say it to me. You can say it to the advisor.
turns.zh: 这是别人也在经历的问题。如果你们在我身上、在我的生活里看到任何让你们担心的举动，你们就该说出来。可以跟我说，也可以跟那位顾问说。

turns.en: But I think it's up to us to sort of open the door for the fact that we know that these are issues and we want the help if someone suspects that it's an issue in our life. Financial institutions are also now on the lookout for this. And the thing to do is to put a trusted person, to name a trusted person on your accounts so that if your financial institutions start to suspect that there's a problem, they have somebody besides you that they can call.
turns.zh: 但我觉得，该由我们自己先把门打开，让大家知道我们清楚这些问题、如果有人怀疑我们的生活里出了这类问题，我们是愿意接受帮助的。金融机构现在也在这方面留心。要做的事，是在你的账户上指定一位你信任的人，这样一旦你的金融机构开始怀疑出了问题，他们有一个可以打给的人，而不只是找你。

turns.en: Another kind of scam that we often hear about with older adults and this ties into the loneliness issue that you were talking about a few minutes ago is romance scams where people meet someone online and get kind of emotionally involved without realizing the other person is looking for money basically. Is there a way family members can look out for that but without being overly controlling of an older relative's relationships?
turns.zh: 还有一种我们常听说、针对老年人的骗局——它跟你几分钟前谈的孤独问题是一回事——就是情感诈骗（romance scams）：人们在网上认识某个人，在情感上陷了进去，却没意识到对方基本就是在盯着钱。家人有没有办法对此留个心眼，又不至于对长辈的感情关系过度干涉？

turns.en: It, oh boy, it is really difficult and the proliferation of romance scams shows just how difficult it is because quite often the older adults do not want to hear it, right?
turns.zh: 哦，天哪，这真的很难。情感诈骗这么泛滥，恰恰说明它有多难，因为很多时候那些老人根本不想听劝，对吧？

turns.en: This is somebody who is paying a lot of attention to them in a way that they have not been paid attention to. In quite some time, the attention feels validating. It makes them feel good and young and important and I think you tread carefully but you don't keep your mouth shut.
turns.zh: 有个人一直在给他们大量的关注，那种关注他们已经很久没有过了。那份被关注让他们觉得自己有价值，让他们感觉良好、感觉自己年轻又重要。所以我觉得你要小心翼翼，但也不能闭口不谈。

turns.en: Sometimes it helps if the advice in this case is not coming from a child but is coming from an advisor. This is one of those cases where I think that the adult child who is worried brings the financial advisor into the conversation to try to help shut the fraud down before it gets bad or worse. I wanted to ask, you know, as you peer forward into your own retirement and you and I have talked about this before, Jean, but how have you adjusted your thinking and the intensive
turns.zh: 有时候，如果这话不是出自子女、而是出自一位顾问，反而会更有用。这就属于那种情况：我觉得忧心忡忡的成年子女把财务顾问也拉进对话，好赶在骗局变得糟糕、变得更糟之前帮忙把它掐掉。我还想问问，当你在展望自己的退休时——Jean，你我以前聊过这个——你那些高强度的

turns.en: research that you put into this book about your own retirement plans, both I would say financial and non-financial? From a financial perspective, I absolutely am looking to put a forever paycheck for myself in place that will cover once again those things that I need but also some of the things that I really want. One of the things that that will allow me to do because I know that my needs have been taken care of and because I also, as my mother did, have a long-term care policy
turns.zh: 研究和为这本书投入的心血，是怎么改变了你对自己退休安排的看法？我说的既包括财务上、也包括非财务上的。财务上来说，我确实正在为自己打造一份永远支票，去覆盖——同样地——我需要的那些，也包括我真心想要的一些东西。有一件我能因此做到的事，就是：我知道我的必需已经保住了，而且我像我母亲一样也有一份长期护理保单，

turns.en: is that that allows me to think differently about how and when I want to help my children. My kids are right around age 30, both of them. My son's a little bit older. My daughter is a little bit younger. They're embarking on their own lives, adult lives, which means having children and buying houses. And as I have gone through this research, I've been thinking about the fact that hopefully I live a really long time, but if I live till, say, 90, they're going to be 60.
turns.zh: 这让我能以不同的方式去想我要怎么、什么时候帮我的孩子。我的两个孩子都在 30 岁上下，儿子大一点，女儿小一点。他们正在开启自己的成年生活，也就是要生孩子、买房。而在我做完这轮研究后，我一直在想：希望我能活很久，可就算我活到 90 岁，那时候他们也 60 岁了。

turns.en: I hope that they don't need my money when they are 60, but I know that they absolutely could use some of it nearer term to do those things like getting a down payment together and helping with 529s for their own kids. And so part of this exercise in putting together a paycheck has allowed me to think a little bit more flexibly in what I want to do for them and also for the causes that I care about. From a non-financial perspective, it really wasn't the research that
turns.zh: 我希望他们 60 岁时用不着我的钱，但我知道，近期他们完全能用到其中一部分——比如凑个首付，或者为他们自己的孩子往 529 账户里添点。所以，打造这份支票这件事的一部分，让我能更灵活地去想我想为他们、也为我关心的那些事业做些什么。非财务的角度来说，真正大幅改变我想法的其实并不是研究，

turns.en: has adjusted my thinking so much, but rather the fact that this year, right around Christmas time, we lost a good friend who just died, not sick, just died, young guy, early 60s. And that really shook us in terms of realizing that you just don't know how much time you have. And we better start doing some of the things that we want to do. I've already said that I'm scared of retirement and I am indeed scared of retirement, not from a financial perspective, but just because I like
turns.zh: 而是今年圣诞节前后，我们失去了一位好朋友。他就那么走了——没生病，就是走了——很年轻，才 60 出头。那真的震撼了我们，让我们意识到：你根本不知道自己还剩多少时间，我们最好现在开始去做一些我们想做的事。我前面已经说过我怕退休，我确实怕退休——不是怕钱不够，而是因为我很喜欢

turns.en: what I do and I'm pretty involved in it. But I have really started thinking about, okay, I think for me, retirement looks like doing a little bit less of what I do today and how to shift into that. Right now, my husband and I have agreed on, we will take one more trip each year.
turns.zh: 我正在做的事，也很投入其中。但我真的开始去想：对我而言，退休大概意味着把今天做的事情稍微少做一点，以及怎么往那个方向过渡。眼下，我和先生达成了一致：我们每年多安排一次旅行。

turns.en: So that's like a baby step, but it's a baby step that was meaningful to him. It's one that I could sort of get behind and we'll look at it from there.
turns.zh: 这算是迈出一小步，但对他来说是有意义的一小步。也是我能认同的一步，剩下的我们走着看。

turns.en: So you did a lot of research and conducted a lot of interviews for the book. As Christine mentioned, it's pretty packed with information about a lot of retirement-related topics. I'm curious, were there any areas where you changed your mind about a given topic after going through the process of doing research for the book? I write in the book about my evolution on annuities.
turns.zh: 你为这本书做了大量研究、做了很多采访。就像 Christine 说的，里面塞满了各种退休相关话题的信息。我很好奇，在为这本书做调研的过程之后，有没有哪个话题是你会改变看法的？我在书里写了我在年金这个问题上的观念演变。

turns.en: I was like many personal finance journalists a hard no on annuities for many, many years. In fact, our financial advisor tried two years ago to sell one to my mother and it would have been a very good product for her. I have learned in hindsight and I would not even let him talk about it. I took a very, very hard pass on that, but I've learned about what these products can do that other products can't. And so my mind has definitely been changed about that. As far as
turns.zh: 我和很多个人理财记者一样，很多很多年对年金都是一口回绝、坚决说不。实际上，我们家的财务顾问两年前曾想向我母亲推销一份年金，那对她本来会是非常合适的产品。事后我才明白，当时我连让他开口都不让，硬是把它给推掉了。但我渐渐了解到这些产品能做到别的做不到的事，所以在这件事上，我的想法确实变了。至于

turns.en: other areas where I've done a complete 180, I don't really think so, but I've learned so much about why we behave the way we behave in retirement, particularly with spending that I think I think I'll be smarter about it when my time actually comes.
turns.zh: 要说还有什么方面我彻底来了个 180 度大转弯，我倒不觉得有；但我学到了太多，关于我们在退休里为什么会那样行事，尤其是花钱这件事，所以我想，等到真轮到我的时候，我大概会更聪明一些。

turns.zh: Jean，我们真高兴你为我们所有人做了这场寻找自我。这本书做得太好了，我们一直很喜欢听你的洞见。非常感谢你来做客。
